Quite a few years ago as a PFY I got a summer job, part of which involved converting a load of files from incredibly old formats (originally created on DOS applications in the 80s) to their newer Microsoft Office equivalents. The word processing files were fairly easy, as were the spreadsheets but there was simply no easy way to convert the presentation files without manually re-creating them. Any attempts at automatic conversion resulted in the layout messing up (they included complex objects like charts in them).

There were at least 20k files, so there was no way I'd even make a dent in them recreating them by hand. I figured I would use a shortcut; I'd export all of the slides as image files and then create new PowerPoints out of those images. I checked with my direct supervisor that it was okay to do this and he gave me the go-ahead; after all, they only wanted to be able to review them, not make changes. I also spoke to the head of the department, who also seemed fine with it.

After about two-thirds of my time there, one of the other employees, MeanGuy, who I had never even spoken to asked about how the file conversions were coming along. This guy was clearly very senior, since he had his own private office (not even the head of the department had a private office). I told him I had completed them and showed him what I had done.

That's not really what I wanted. I was expecting people would be able to edit them.

After a bit more talking it becomes clear that he had been the one to want the project done in the first place, but had never even thought to talk to me about what his goal was. At the time I just apologized that it was not what he was after, but I really wished I had asked why he hadn't decided to meet me earlier since he was the one who commissioned the project. I also wished I had asked why he even wanted to be able to edit 20 year old presentations that were based off of data that was now very outdated.

I was pretty upset for a while, thinking I had disappointed someone high up in the company. After noticing I wasn't very happy one of the other staff in the department gave me a bit of a history lesson. It turns out that MeanGuy had actually been working in the department for the longest but was widely disliked so a much less experienced employee had been promoted to manager. This had made MeanGuy even more bitter and dislikable than before. The only reason MeanGuy had his own office was because he was basically impossible to work with and everyone wanted to keep him out of the way.

I learned some very valuable lessons from what was otherwise one of the most boring jobs I've ever had: always find out who you are really working for and never assume someone is senior because they have their own office.

Sorry if this was not tech-supporty enough, but I figured this subverse desperately needed some content and I thought this might fit, even though it's not the most interesting of stories.
